name: Greek Vase
basis: why: one black glaze and the red of the clay, detail scratched or drawn; how: two-tone cut, black-figure incision or red-figure reserve, meander border
note: Greek 'glaze' is a refined gloss slip; family glaze is the nearest.

lumenary.blurb: The picture painted onto the side of an ancient Greek vase. In black-figure the shapes are glossy black glaze on orange clay, with fine lines scratched through to the clay; in red-figure it is the other way round. Meander borders, the curve of the pot and the cracks of two thousand years finish it.

facts.era: Black-figure from about 700 BC, red-figure from about 530 BC
facts.bestOn: Pictures with strong shapes and clear dark or light figures

why: Greek vase painters had no colours to mix, only one black glaze and the red of the clay. So every figure had to be a silhouette, and detail had to be scratched or drawn as line. That limit made the style: bold shapes, the profile view, and a border of repeating pattern to hold the picture in. A photograph pressed through it loses its shading and keeps its outline, which is what a silhouette is for.
how: Lift the local contrast, then cut the picture into two tones at a level set by how much is to be painted.
In black-figure the dark shapes are glaze on bare clay; in red-figure the light shapes are the clay and the ground is glazed.
Scratch fine lines through the glaze to the clay for black-figure, or draw them in glaze on the clay for red-figure.
Add red and white over the glaze where the picture is warm or cool, as painters did for cloth and skin.
Draw a meander border above and below, shade the pot darker towards its sides, and age it with stains and cracks.
history: Black-figure pottery began in Corinth about 700 BC and was perfected in Athens, where painters drew figures in a slip that turned black in a three-stage firing and scratched details through to the clay. Around 530 BC the Andokides Painter and his circle reversed it: red-figure left the figures the colour of the clay and painted the ground, so that details could be drawn with a brush. The meander, or Greek key, is a running hook pattern and among the oldest decorations of the Greek world.
uses: Museum shop prints and book covers
Packaging for olive oil, wine and food
Posters for classical events and plays
terms: A vase painting style in which figures are black glaze on the clay and details are scratched through it.
A vase painting style in which figures are left the colour of the clay and the ground is painted black.
A continuous line that turns back on itself in right angles, also called the Greek key.
paragraphs: The picture is first given a local contrast boost, T = l + 0.85 (l - l_bar), with l_bar a wide blur, after a small blur has taken out the grain. A threshold t, from 0.16 to 0.62 with the slider for how much is painted, cuts it in two with a soft edge of 0.035. For black-figure the glaze mask is G = smoothstep(t + 0.035, t - 0.035, T), the dark shapes; for red-figure it is 1 - smoothstep(1 - t - 0.035, 1 - t + 0.035, T), the ground. The mask is blurred and sharpened again with smoothstep(0.4, 0.6) so that outlines are smooth. The border is a row of meander hooks drawn as a stroked path on a separate canvas, and added to the mask.

The clay is a base colour times a mottling of fractal noise (plus or minus 10%), a fine grain and a slight darkening next to the glaze; the glaze is near black with a faint sheen of noise. Scratched lines are where the Sobel gradient of the brightness exceeds a limit that falls as the scratch slider rises, together with thin dark features; they are mixed in as clay colour inside the glaze for black-figure, and as glaze inside the clay for red-figure. For the added colours, the blurred picture is read where the glaze is: if its chroma is above 0.14 it is painted crimson where it is warmer than blue, and white where it is cooler. Finally the pot is shaded by 1 - 0.62 c s^2.3, where s is the distance from the centre line (0 to 1) and c the curve slider, with a soft highlight on the left, and aged by stains, a net of cracks from the edges of a cellular (Voronoi) pattern, and a few chips of bare clay.

equations.note: Black-figure: the glaze mask G is where the boosted brightness T falls below the threshold t.
The curve of the pot: u is the position across the picture (0 to 1) and c the curve slider.
A net of cracks from a Voronoi pattern: d_1 and d_2 are the distances to the nearest and second nearest points, and sigma is the picture scale.

presets.text: Red-figure on pale clay gives the crisp look of a classical vase painting.
More painted area and strong scratching keep the details of a face.
Less age and no border make it a clean, modern pot design.
